analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to regulate and clean up PFAS "forever chemicals" in drinking water, air, and waste.
analysis.headline: The House passed the PFAS Action Act 247-159 in January 2020, but the Senate never acted on it, so the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made "forever chemicals" used in nonstick cookware, water-repellent clothing, carpets, and firefighting foam that do not break down and have been linked to health problems. This bill would have required the EPA to set a national drinking water standard for PFAS, designate the two most notorious ones (PFOA and PFOS) as hazardous substances requiring cleanup, order toxicity testing of all PFAS, restrict new PFAS from entering the market, set limits on industrial discharges into water, and give grants to help water systems — prioritizing small and disadvantaged communities — pay for treatment. The House passed it, but the Senate never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from public water systems would get enforceable national limits on PFAS in their tap water and, in time, treatment; communities near contaminated sites would see mandatory cleanup; small and disadvantaged communities get federal money for testing and treatment; firefighters get guidance to reduce exposure to PFAS foam; consumers get a label to identify PFAS-free cookware, clothing, and furniture; and households on private wells get a testing-information website.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to set a national drinking water standard for PFAS, with a deadline for the rule and health advisories for unregulated PFAS [S3, S5, Sec. 5].
Designates PFOA and PFOS as hazardous substances, which forces cleanup of contaminated sites and assigns responsibility for releases [S3, S5, Sec. 2].
Requires comprehensive toxicity testing of all PFAS and a five-year moratorium on new PFAS entering commerce without review [S3, S5, Secs. 3-4].
Authorizes $125 million a year in grants to help water systems — prioritizing disadvantaged and disproportionately exposed communities — pay for treatment technology to remove PFAS [S5, Sec. 7].

Adds PFAS to the list of hazardous air pollutants, sets disposal rules for PFAS waste and firefighting foam, requires industry to disclose PFAS sent to treatment plants, and creates a label for PFAS-free products so consumers can identify them [S3, S5, Secs. 8-13].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and industrial dischargers would bear testing costs, disclosure requirements, discharge limits, and cleanup liability; water systems would face compliance costs, offset by federal grants and a five-year penalty holiday.

drawbacks.text: The bill barred EPA from imposing financial penalties on PFAS drinking-water violations for the first five years after a regulation takes effect, so water systems that exceed the new limits would face no monetary consequence early on [S5, Sec. 6].
It exempted airports from liability for cleanup costs from PFAS released through required use of firefighting foam, shifting those costs away from airport operators [S4, S5, Sec. 2(c)].

Complying with new drinking-water limits and monitoring would cost public water systems money; the bill offsets this with federal grants rather than fully covering it, and some costs could reach water customers over time [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: PFAS are linked to serious illness and persist in the environment indefinitely, and communities near military and industrial sites have been drinking contaminated water for decades. The main costs fall on chemical manufacturers and water systems, and the bill shields small and disadvantaged water systems from testing costs and from penalties for five years — an honest acknowledgment that compliance takes time. Weakenings (the airport liability exemption and the five-year enforcement moratorium) are real concessions but do not erase the bill's core protections. On balance the bill would have helped ordinary people at the expense of a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 247-159 in January 2020, but the Senate referred it to its Environment and Public Works Committee and never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: A Republican motion to recommit — a last-chance amendment — failed 187-219 on January 10, 2020, with 182 of 198 Republicans voting yes and only 4 Democrats crossing over [S7, S8].
The House passed the bill the same day, 247-159: 223 of 231 Democrats voted yes while only 24 of 198 Republicans did [S7, S9].
The Senate received the bill on January 13, 2020 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was taken [S1, S7].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no Senate vote ever taken [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers, industrial dischargers, and water utilities avoided mandatory federal standards and the compliance and testing costs that would have come with them.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was lopsided but split by party: 223 of 231 Democrats voted yes while only 24 of 198 Republicans did; the failed motion to recommit was even sharper, with 182 of 198 Republicans voting yes and all but 4 Democrats voting no.

industries.industry: PFAS manufacturers and the chemical industry
industries.note: The bill requires toxicity testing of all PFAS, blocks new PFAS from entering commerce for five years without review, and makes PFAS producers report what they make and discharge — costs the industry had long avoided under the current system.

Utilities would face a national PFAS drinking water standard and monitoring costs, but the bill pays testing costs for small systems, bars penalties for the first five years, and offers treatment grants — so the burden is substantially offset.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (chemical, pulp and paper, textile plants)
industries.note: The bill requires effluent limits and disclosure of PFAS sent to treatment works, raising compliance costs, but grants help publicly owned treatment works implement the standards.

An amendment exempted federally funded airports from liability for PFAS cleanup from required firefighting foam use, shifting those costs to others; airports still face guidance to minimize PFAS foam use.

industries.industry: Firefighting foam manufacturers and firefighting sector
industries.note: PFAS foam disposal becomes regulated as hazardous waste and first responders get guidance to reduce exposure, but the bill does not ban the foam outright.
